name: RME
strapline: Explore beliefs. Think carefully. Listen respectfully.
intro: Religious and Moral Education explores religious and non-religious worldviews, values and questions about human life. You are never asked to adopt a belief or disclose personal beliefs. Use evidence, acknowledge diversity within traditions and disagree respectfully with ideas. BGE enquiries below are suggestions. Senior qualifications are called Religious, Moral and Philosophical Studies (RMPS), with departmental choices within national areas.

bge.title: Belonging and belief
bge.question: What shapes how people see the world?
bge.task: Create a fictional character with several influences on their worldview. Explain why no single label describes everything about them.
bge.extend: Compare two first-person accounts from the same tradition without assuming they represent everyone.

bge.title: What makes an action right?
bge.question: Should we judge intentions or consequences?
bge.task: Consider a fictional promise broken to help someone in urgent need. Present a reason for keeping the promise and a reason for breaking it.
bge.extend: Explain which principle matters most in your judgement and test it against another situation.

bge.title: Celebration, story and symbol
bge.question: Why can a symbol mean more than it shows?
bge.task: Choose a teacher-approved celebration. Explain the meaning of one practice using a reliable source from that community.
bge.extend: Find a different account and explain how practice varies.

bge.title: A fairer community
bge.question: What do we owe to one another?
bge.task: Design an inclusive community event. Explain how two decisions support participation and respect.
bge.extend: Identify a conflict between two reasonable priorities and propose a justified compromise.

senior.title: Religious, Moral and Philosophical Studies
senior.explain: Study the selected religion and issues through nationally specified areas. The department confirms options; these are not personal faith tests.
senior.assessment: Internal units; National 4 also includes an added value assignment.

senior.title: Religious, Moral and Philosophical Studies
senior.explain: Explain beliefs, analyse responses and support conclusions. Specific religion and issue options are departmental choices within the specification.
senior.assessment: Question paper and assignment. Consult the current course page and assessment instructions.

senior.title: Religious, Moral and Philosophical Studies
senior.explain: Develop deeper analysis and evaluation of arguments and perspectives. Use accurate examples while acknowledging diversity within worldviews.
senior.assessment: Question papers and assignment under current national arrangements; teachers confirm selected options.

skills.title: Describe accurately
skills.explain: Explain a view in terms its holder could recognise.
skills.try: Summarise a source without adding your judgement.
skills.check: Have you avoided “all believers think” when views vary?

skills.title: Build an argument
skills.explain: A conclusion needs reasons and relevant examples.
skills.try: Write a claim, a reason and an example illustrating that reason.
skills.check: Does the example actually support the claim?

skills.title: Evaluate fairly
skills.explain: Consider the strongest version of another view.
skills.try: Write an objection and a possible reply.
skills.check: Explain whether the reply answers the objection rather than repeating your opinion.

skills.title: Listen with respect
skills.try: Paraphrase a partner’s argument before responding.
skills.check: Ask if your summary is fair; challenge the idea without judging the person.

practice.question: “Most people in our group support the rule, so the rule must be morally right.” Is that enough?
practice.hint: Popularity and moral justification are different kinds of claim.
practice.answer: No. Agreement tells us what a group thinks, but a moral defence also needs reasons, such as fairness, wellbeing or rights. A majority can overlook the interests of a minority.
practice.extend: Offer one reason for the rule and one possible objection.

practice.question: A source says one member of a religion volunteers every week. Can we conclude all members do the same?
practice.hint: Think about the limits of a single example.
practice.answer: No. The source provides evidence about that individual. It may illustrate a belief in service, but frequency and motivation differ among people. Use careful language such as “some members”.
practice.extend: What evidence would help investigate a wider pattern?

practice.question: A fictional school has funding for either a quiet study space or extra sports equipment. Give a fair argument for each and a justified decision.
practice.hint: Identify the needs each choice meets and who might be affected.
practice.answer: Study space may support learners without quiet space at home; equipment may support physical wellbeing and participation. Either conclusion can be justified if it weighs need, access and likely benefit. An unsupported preference is weaker.
practice.extend: Suggest a compromise and explain what it would fail to solve.

resources.title: Interfaith Scotland: youth and schools
resources.task: Use a first-person resource to record one belief, one practice and one question; avoid generalising to everyone.

resources.title: Understanding Humanism
resources.task: Explain a humanist approach to a moral question using its own educational resources.

resources.title: United Nations: Universal Declaration of Human Rights
resources.task: Choose an article and explain a practical situation in which it matters.

resources.title: UK Parliament learning
resources.task: Explore a rights or law resource, then distinguish what is legal from what is morally justified.

resources.title: Official RMPS resources
resources.task: Select your level and compare a practice response with official marking guidance.

ipad.title: An argument map
steps: Write a clearly worded moral question.
Map two views with reasons, examples and objections.
Record a conclusion that weighs the strongest points.
ipad.evidence: A balanced map and a justified personal conclusion; no disclosure of faith required.

ipad.title: A worldview glossary
steps: Choose eight terms used in class.
Add a definition, reliable source and example.
Use audio or a home-language gloss to support understanding.
ipad.evidence: An accurate glossary that distinguishes description from judgement.

ipad.title: Reflective audio
steps: Record what you first thought and what evidence challenged it.
Add a transcript and a remaining question.
ipad.evidence: A short reflection showing open-mindedness and respectful reasoning.

parentTip: Ask your young person to explain a reason for a view they do not share. Praise fair representation and thoughtful questions. They should never feel required to share private family beliefs to complete a learning task.
